key_features.classic_presentation: Acute diverticulitis presents with left lower quadrant (LLQ) pain that is constant and progressively worsening. Low-grade fever and changes in bowel habits (diarrhea or constipation) are common. More common in older adults (>50 years).
key_features.typical_demographics: Incidence increases with age. 50% of people >60 have diverticulosis, 10-25% develop diverticulitis. Western diet, low fiber increase risk.
key_features.pathophysiology_brief: Inflammation/infection of colonic diverticulum (outpouching) leads to microperforation, abscess formation, or free perforation.

diagnostic_questions.context: LLQ pain is classic (85%). Right-sided occurs in 15% (Asian populations higher, cecal diverticula).
Pain is constant and progressively worsens over hours to days.
Low-grade fever (100-102°F) present in most cases. High fever suggests abscess or perforation.
Changes in bowel habits common (60%). Can be diarrhea, constipation, or alternating.
Much more common in older adults. Rare under age 40.
Symptoms typically develop over 1-3 days, not sudden onset.

differential_diagnosis.key_difference: RLQ pain (not LLQ), younger age typically
More gradual, weight loss, blood in stool over weeks

typical_management: Mild: outpatient antibiotics, clear liquid diet. Moderate-severe: admission, IV antibiotics, NPO. Complicated: surgical consultation for abscess drainage or resection.
disposition: Uncomplicated: may treat outpatient with close follow-up. Complicated: emergency department, likely admission.
patient_education: Diverticulitis is inflammation of small pouches in the colon. It requires antibiotics and bowel rest. Most cases respond to treatment, but complications like abscess or perforation can occur.
